title: JavaScript Core: Closures, Event Loop, Promises

scenes.say: Three timers, one loop, and the output is three, three, three. You'll predict the exact print order of any async snippet. Most candidates can't.
Today you will do three things. Explain closures, scope, and this. Predict the order of timers, promises, and awaits. And handle a failing fetch with try and catch.
lines: Predict the order of any async snippet

scenes.title: Why does this loop print 3, 3, 3?
scenes.statement: A loop schedules three timers. Each one logs the counter. You expect 0, 1, 2. Explain what prints and fix it.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, three timers in a var loop. We want zero, one, two, but we get three, three, three.

scenes.head: Think of a backpack
scenes.say: Think of a backpack. When a function is created, it packs the variables around it. Wherever the function travels, the backpack goes along. Whenever it runs, it reads its own backpack. That backpack is a closure.

scenes.head: Each call gets its own backpack
scenes.say: Here's a closure in code. Make counter creates count, and returns a small function. Normally count would vanish when make counter returns. It doesn't: the small function keeps it. A twice gives one, two. B has its own backpack, so one. Nobody else can touch count. That is private state, and callbacks and memoization use the same trick.

scenes.head: One `i`, three callbacks
scenes.say: Here's why the loop fails. With var, there is one i for the whole loop. Three callbacks, all pointing at the same box. The loop runs first, and i climbs to three. Later the timers fire. Each callback reads the same box, and sees three.
Your turn. Change var to let, and run it again. Same loop, same three timers. What prints? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Same loop, but `let i`. What do the three timers print?

scenes.head: `let` gives each pass its own `i`
scenes.say: Zero, one, two. With let, every pass gets a fresh i, so each callback closes over its own box. That is block scope. Var is scoped to the whole function, let to the block. Run it, and the timers print zero, one, two.

scenes.title: Why does a detached method fail?
scenes.statement: A method returns this.name. Called as u.hi() it works. Copy it to f and call f(), and it breaks.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, call u dot hi, then copy the method and call it bare. We want one answer and one crash.

scenes.head: The word I
scenes.say: Think of the word I. Ada says it: I is Ada. Bo says it: I is Bo. Nobody says it: I is nothing. In code, I is this.

scenes.head: A detached method loses `this`
scenes.say: Here is the class. A dot call, u dot hi, works: Ada. Copy the method to f and call it bare, and this is lost. Inside a class that means undefined, so it throws a type error. Bind locks this to u. Now it works again.
Your turn. Object h has the name Bo, and it borrows the method from u. What does h dot hi return? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `const h = { name: 'Bo', hi: u.hi }`. What does `h.hi()` return?

scenes.head: `this`, in four kinds of call
scenes.say: Bo. This is decided by the call, not by where the method was written. A dot call: this is the object before the dot. A bare call: this is lost. Bind: this is locked. Arrow functions have no this of their own, they use the one around them.
rows: none of its own: the outer one

scenes.title: Predict the print order
scenes.statement: Four lines: a log, a timer of zero, a promise callback, another log. In what order do they print?

example.input: log 1, timer logs 2, then logs 3, log 4

scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, four lines: log one, timer, promise, log four. We want the order.

scenes.head: A shop with one cashier
scenes.say: Think of a shop with one cashier. That is JavaScript: one thread, one customer at a time. The priority lane holds microtasks: promise callbacks and await. The normal line holds tasks: timers, clicks, network. Priority lane always goes first.

scenes.head: The loop, step by step
scenes.say: Run the script top to bottom. Line one goes on the stack, and prints one. Line two, set timeout. The browser holds the timer, then queues its callback in the task queue. Line three, the promise. Its callback lands in the microtask queue. Line four prints four. The stack is empty. Microtasks go first, and three prints. Then one task, and two prints.

scenes.head: The snippet, for real
scenes.say: Now the real code. A log helper that prints on one line. Log one. A timer of zero, which still waits for the task queue. A promise callback, a microtask. Then log four. Run it: one, four, three, two.
Your turn. Add a second promise then, right after the first. It logs five. Where does five land? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Script: log 1, timer logs 2, then logs 3, then logs 5, log 4. Order?

scenes.head: The loop, step by step
scenes.say: One, four, three, five, two. Both promise callbacks sit in the microtask queue, and the stack is empty. First three runs, and prints. Then five runs, and prints. The microtask queue is empty. Only now does the timer run, and two prints.

scenes.head: `await` is a microtask too
scenes.say: Async functions follow the same rules. Everything before the first await runs right away: that prints s. At the await, the rest becomes a microtask, and the caller moves on. So A, s, B. Then the microtasks, in queue order: w, then P. The timer comes last.

output.text: A s B w P T

scenes.head: Follow-ups on the event loop
scenes.say: Common follow-ups. Is set timeout zero immediate? No, it runs after every microtask. Microtask examples: then, await, queue microtask. Task examples: timers, clicks, network. A long loop blocks everything, even clicks. And microtasks that keep queueing more microtasks starve rendering.

scenes.title: Load a user when the server fails
scenes.statement: Fetch a user from an API. When the server answers 404, the code must not crash. Return a safe value.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, fetch user seven, and the server answers four oh four. We want the error caught, not a crash.

scenes.head: A promise is a buzzer
scenes.say: Think of ordering pizza. A promise is your buzzer: it starts pending. Later it settles exactly once. Fulfilled: the pizza arrives. Or rejected: sold out. Never changes after that. Await means sit and wait.

scenes.head: Errors: try and catch
scenes.say: Await pauses this function until the promise settles. A rejection becomes a normal throw, so try and catch just works. One trap: fetch only rejects when the network fails. A four oh four still resolves. So check res dot ok, and throw yourself. The catch then handles both.
Your turn. Two independent calls take a hundred milliseconds each. You await one, then the other. How long in total? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Await call A (100 ms), then call B (100 ms). Total time?

scenes.head: One by one, or together
scenes.say: About two hundred. The second call does not even start until the first finishes. The fix: start both, and wait together with promise dot all. It finishes when the slowest does. Serial two hundred, together a hundred.

scenes.head: Promise follow-ups
scenes.say: Follow-ups. If promise dot all fails? It rejects as soon as one rejects. Want every result anyway? All settled reports each one. Does await block? No, only that function pauses. Promise versus callback? Promises chain and share one error path. Common mistake: forgetting await, or awaiting in a loop that could run in parallel.
rows: rejects as soon as one rejects
missing `await`, or awaiting in a loop

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is a closure? A function plus the variables it was created with. Why use one? Private state and memoization. Downside? Kept variables can leak. Var versus let? Function scoped versus block scoped. Arrow versus normal this? Arrows use the outer one.
rows: a function + the variables it was created with
private state, memoization; kept variables can leak
arrow uses the outer `this`; normal follows the call

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Is JavaScript async? Single threaded. The browser waits, the loop runs callbacks. Order? Sync code, then all microtasks, then one task. Examples? Then and await versus timers and clicks. Common mistake? Thinking timeout zero is immediate.
rows: single thread; browser waits, loop runs callbacks
sync code, all microtasks, then one task

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Promise versus callback? Chaining and one error path. States? Pending, then fulfilled or rejected, once. Errors? Await with try and catch, and check res dot ok. Parallel? Promise dot all, or all settled for every result.
rows: chains, one error path, no pyramid
pending, then fulfilled or rejected, once

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Do these next. Predict, then run, five snippets that mix timers, promises, and await. Explain this for a dot call, a bare call, bind, and an arrow. Then write load user with try and catch, and add promise dot all.
rows: Predict, then run, 5 snippets mixing timers, promises, `await`
Explain `this`: dot call, bare call, `bind`, arrow

scenes.say: So say this. A closure is a function plus the variables it was created with. Run sync code, then every microtask, then one task. And await turns a rejection into a throw, so use try and catch.
